```bash
bun "<skill-folder>/references/call-file.ts" create_field .tmp_deploy/departments-fields.json
```

#### Computed defaults

The platform works these out for each record a write creates. Write the word on its own:

| Format | `default_value` | A record that leaves the field out gets |
|---|---|---|
| `date` | `today`, `tomorrow`, `yesterday` | that day, in UTC |
| `date-time` | `now`; `today`, `tomorrow`, `yesterday` | the moment of the insert; midnight UTC of that day |
| `time` | `now` | the time of day of the insert, in UTC |
| `uuid` | `gen_random_uuid()` | a new UUID |
| `reference` or `parent` to `users` | `CURRENT_USER` | the signed-in user's id |

- **Other spellings mean the same.** `$today`, `$now`, `$user_id`, `CURRENT_DATE`, `now()` and the other SQL date and time keywords, in any case, are read the same where the format fits, and a live field may carry any of them. Write the words above: a shell expands `$today` in an unquoted heredoc and leaves an empty default. A day word with anything else (`today + 7`, `tomorrow 09:00`), and `today`, `tomorrow` or `yesterday` on a `time` field, which takes only `now`, are refused (`90284`).
- **A default cannot count days.** A date some days after the insert is sent by the writer. A date that follows from another stored date of the record is a computed field (`jsonlogic.md` → "Date operators"), never one computed from `$today`.
- **`CURRENT_USER` is the signed-in user only on a `reference` or `parent` field to `users`.**
  - A value the write sends wins, an explicit `null` included, so the writer can name another user. A field a gate relies on is stamped by the command instead (`rbac.md` → "Controls on a gate").
  - A write with no signed-in user leaves it NULL, so a required field refuses that write (`90258`).
  - Records that already exist never take it. On a table with records, add a required one as `default`, fill the records, then make it `required` (`90259` otherwise); a `parent` one can be added only while the table is empty.
  - On any other field the platform refuses it (`90283`), except on a text field, where it stores the database role name, the same for every user; `call-file.ts` refuses that. `$user_id` the platform refuses on every field but a `reference` or `parent` to `users`, a text field included.
- **Who opened a record.** The field that records who created, opened, requested or reported a record is a `reference` to `users` with `default_value` `CURRENT_USER` and `input_type` `default`: the form starts with the signed-in user, and the writer can name another. It is named for the domain's verb, `<verb>_by_user_id`, and an entity has one. A field that names who works on, approves or is assigned to a record has no default. A gate that needs the requester uses this field (`rbac.md` → "Controls on a gate").

### Enum values and labels

An `enum_values` entry is either a plain value (`"draft"`) or a `{"value", "label"}` object (`{"value": "on_hold", "label": "On hold"}`), and the two forms can be mixed. An object may also carry an optional `description`, `color` (an HTML color) and `icon` (a Lucide icon name); these are UI hints only. **Records store the value; the label, description, color and icon are only what the UI shows.** Rules:

- Write every entry as an object with a `label` and a `color`. The label is the value in words, in sentence case (`{"value": "checked_out", "label": "Checked out"}`), or the full term for a code or an abbreviation (`{"value": "nda", "label": "Non-disclosure agreement"}`); an entry without a label shows its raw value. The color follows "Enum colors" below. An object always carries `label`.
- **Give every entry of every enum an `icon` that fits its meaning.** Take it from "Enum icons" below; put every label that fits no row there in one `lucide-icon-finder.ts --batch -` call ("Icons are Lucide icons"). When the finder finds nothing that fits, the entry has no icon. Never write an icon name from memory: `call-file.ts` refuses one that is not a Lucide icon.
- `description` is the exception: add it only when the label is not self-describing (an internal code, a term of art, two choices a user could confuse). A label like "Approved" needs none.
- Never an object map like `{"draft": "Draft"}`: `enum_values` is always an array.
- Writes, filters, `default_value` and JsonLogic compare against the **value**, never the label. Only the value reaches the CHECK constraint and the column default.
- Reading `enum_values` back (or the `enum` list of a property in `get_schema`) returns the entries as defined, so an object comes back as an object with any `description`, `color` and `icon` it carries: take its `value`. `get_schema` also lists `""` for an enum that is not required.
- Changing only a label, description, color or icon is cosmetic (records keep their values); adding, removing or renaming a value is a schema change (see Safe Evolution).
- `update_field` replaces the whole `enum_values` array, so send every entry back with all of its keys; an entry sent without its `color` loses it. Removing a value still in use is refused (`23514`).

```json
   "default_value": "msa", "input_type": "required", "width": "default"},
  {"table_name": "contracts", "field_name": "workflow_state", "title": "Status", "format": "enum",
   "enum_values": [
```

#### Enum icons

Take the icon of the row whose meaning the entry's label carries. Put every label that fits no row in one `lucide-icon-finder.ts --batch -` call and take the first hit that clearly matches the meaning.

| Entry meaning | `icon` | Entry meaning | `icon` |
|---|---|---|---|
| draft, new | `file-pen` | approved, done | `circle-check` |
| submitted | `send` | completed | `check-check` |
| in review, pending, waiting | `clock` | active, in use | `circle-play` |
| upcoming | `calendar-clock` | on hold, suspended, idle | `circle-pause` |
| renegotiated | `refresh-cw` | blocked | `ban` |
| trial | `hourglass` | canceled, failed | `circle-x` |
| rejected | `x` | expired, retired, revoked, inactive, void | `circle-slash` |
| overdue | `circle-alert` | on leave | `tree-palm` |
| disputed | `scale` | left | `log-out` |
| low (level) | `signal-low` | medium (level) | `signal-medium` |
| high (level) | `signal-high` | critical (level) | `siren` |
| paid | `circle-dollar-sign` | | |

#### Enum colors

Write each hex in lowercase, exactly as listed. No two entries of one enum share a color.

**Enums whose values are states or levels**, `workflow_state` among them, take each entry's color by its meaning. When two or more entries share a meaning (`submitted` and `in_review` are both waiting), the first takes the `color`, the next ones the shades in order:

| Entry meaning | `color` | Shades |
|---|---|---|
| draft, new, initial | `#64748b` | `#475569` · `#94a3b8` |
| active, open, in progress | `#3b82f6` | `#2563eb` · `#60a5fa` |
| waiting, on hold, pending | `#f59e0b` | `#d97706` · `#fbbf24` |
| done, approved, closed as success | `#22c55e` | `#16a34a` · `#4ade80` |
| canceled, failed, rejected | `#ef4444` | `#dc2626` · `#f87171` |
| levels: low · medium · high · critical | `#64748b` · `#3b82f6` · `#f59e0b` · `#ef4444` | |

Past the listed shades, a further entry of that meaning gets another shade of the same hue that the enum does not use yet.

**Every other enum:** an entry whose label carries one of the meanings above takes that color (`approved` → `#22c55e`). Red, amber and green go only to such entries, never to an entry whose label does not relate to them (never red for `approved`). Every other entry takes the next color of this set that the enum does not use yet, in order:

| # | Color | `color` |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | blue | `#3b82f6` |
| 2 | pink | `#ec4899` |
| 3 | teal | `#14b8a6` |
| 4 | slate | `#64748b` |
| 5 | cyan | `#06b6d4` |
| 6 | purple | `#a855f7` |

Purple is last because next to blue it is easy to miss; an enum with few entries never gets it. Once the set is used up, each further entry gets a new hex that is not red, amber or green in hue.

### `cube_type` Values

Controls how a field participates in OLAP cube generation (only relevant when the entity has `cube_mode: "auto"`).

| Value | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `disabled` | Field excluded from cube |
| `auto` | **Default.** System infers dimension or measure from `format` |
| `dimension` | Explicit grouping axis (e.g. category, region, status) |
| `measure` | Explicit numeric aggregation (e.g. revenue, count) |

When to set `cube_type` explicitly:

- `dimension`: categorical fields the user will group or filter by (status, country, product type)
- `measure`: numeric fields the user will aggregate (amount, quantity, duration)
- `disabled`: fields that should be excluded from cube queries even if `cube_mode: "auto"` is set on the entity (e.g. internal audit fields, raw foreign keys)
- `auto`: default; leave unset unless the system inference is incorrect

### Example: Add Fields to an Entity

All new fields of an entity go into **one** `create_field` call — `data` is an array, and the items may carry different keys (`searchable` on one, `precision` on another, `enum_values` + `default_value` on a third; a key omitted from an item takes the column default). One request, one transaction, one array back. `.tmp_deploy/products-fields.json`:

```json
{
  "data": [
    {
      "table_name": "products",
      "field_name": "description",
      "title": "Description",
      "format": "multiline",
      "width": "default",
      "input_type": "default",
      "searchable": true
    },
    {
      "table_name": "products",
      "field_name": "price",
      "title": "Price",
      "format": "number",
      "precision": 2,
      "width": "default",
      "input_type": "default"
    },
    {
      "table_name": "products",
      "field_name": "workflow_state",
      "title": "Status",
      "format": "enum",
      "enum_values": [
        {"value": "draft", "label": "Draft", "color": "#64748b", "icon": "file-pen"},
        {"value": "active", "label": "Active", "color": "#3b82f6", "icon": "circle-play"},
        {"value": "discontinued", "label": "Discontinued", "color": "#475569", "icon": "circle-slash"}
      ],
      "default_value": "draft",
      "width": "default",
      "input_type": "required"
    }
  ]
}
```

```bash
bun "<skill-folder>/references/call-file.ts" create_field .tmp_deploy/products-fields.json
```

No `field_order`: the platform places each new field after the entity's existing fields, in array order, so list the items in the order they should display.

Three separate `create_field` calls for the three fields would be three round trips with no atomicity — the failure the batching rule (Golden Rule 7) names. Duplicate check first, in one read: `read_field '{"filters": "table_name=eq.products&field_name=in.(description,price,workflow_state)"}'`.

### All Field Properties

| Property | Type | Notes |
|----------|------|-------|
| `table_name` | string | Target entity, required |
| `field_name` | string | Snake_case identifier. Renaming is supported but think twice: views, integrations, and saved queries reference the field by name. What a rename changes in rules: "Safe Evolution Patterns" → High-Risk. |
| `title` | string | Human-readable label shown in UI |
| `description` | string | Explains what the field represents |
| `format` | string | Changeable only to a format with the same physical database type (e.g., one string format can swap to another string format; `int32` to `int64` is refused with `90223`). See format table above. |
| `width` | string | `default` (default), `s`, `m`, `w` |
| `input_type` | string | `default`, `required`, `readonly`, `disabled`, `hidden` |
| `field_order` | integer | Display position in the UI. **Omit it on create**: the platform gives each new field the next position after the entity's existing fields, in array order. Set it only to put a field at a specific position (on create, or later with `update_field`), and read the entity's live `field_order` values first: the auto-created fields already hold positions (the label field sits at 20), and a tie is not an error, the UI just renders the tied fields in an unpredictable order. Choose a value strictly between the two live neighbors the field should sit between (e.g. 25 between 20 and 30), or above the highest value below 900000 to put it last. The automatic numbering ignores values from 900000 up (`created_at` and `updated_at` sit at 999998 and 999999); keep every other field below 900000. |
| `searchable` | boolean | Adds this field to the entity's full-text search index |
| `unique_value` | boolean | Enforces uniqueness at database level through a partial unique index: for string formats, `NULL` and `''` are exempt. See `### unique_value` above. |
| `enum_values` | array | Required when `format: "enum"`: the allowed entries, each a value or a `{"value", "label"}` object with an optional `description`, `color` and `icon`. Records and `default_value` hold the value, never the label; never an object map. See "Enum values and labels" above. |
| `precision` | integer (0–18) | For `format: "number"` only, number of digits after the decimal point in the generated `NUMERIC` column. Defaults to `2` (suits money and most measured quantities). Set higher (e.g. `4`–`6`) for tax rates, FX rates, or scientific values; `0` for integer-like counts that still want NUMERIC semantics. A change on an existing field alters the column: lowering it rounds the stored values, and any change rewrites the table under an exclusive lock (see "Safe Evolution Patterns"). |
| `default_value` | string | Override for the platform's auto-default. Only set when the auto-default is wrong for the domain. See `### default_value` above for the auto-default table per format, the 200-character limit and the computed defaults. Stored as text: a number or boolean is converted (`1` → `"1"`, `true` → `"true"`), a JSON array or object to its JSON (`{}` → `"{}"`). |
| `reference_table` | string | Target entity's `table_name` for `reference`/`parent` fields |
| `reference_delete_mode` | string | `restrict`, `clear`, or `cascade`. On an `is_a` entity never `cascade` (`90249`): set `restrict` or `clear` explicitly, on `parent` fields too. |
| `relationship_label` | string | Verb for the relationship, set on every `reference` and `parent` field in the same `create_field` call that creates it; omitted, the platform writes `has`. Read it as `<Referenced Entity> <label> <Holding Entity>` (e.g. `"employs"` on `employees.department_id`). Used as the arrow label in module diagrams and in navigation labels. See "Relationship labels". |
| `singular_label_parent` | string | `parent` fields only. The noun in the add button of this field's child list on the parent's page: `"Permission"` gives "Add Permission". |
| `plural_label_parent` | string | `parent` fields only. The title of the button on the parent's page that opens this field's child list: `"Permissions"` gives "Permissions…". Empty, the button uses the child entity's plural label (an Entity page shows "Fields…"). Set the pair on every `parent` field of a junction, and when one child has two or more `parent` fields to the same parent. See "Relationship labels". |
| `cube_type` | string | OLAP cube participation: `disabled`, `auto` (default), `dimension`, `measure`. See `### cube_type Values` above. |
| `catalog_field_code` | string | Core provenance column: stable design-time field identity (the blueprint field name, e.g. `status`), the field-rename join key. Write-once: set on create or filled once while empty, then never changed. Empty = not generated from a catalog spec. See "Platform provenance / meta columns" above. |

## Relationships

### Choosing the Right Format

**What the format does in the app.** A `parent` child is a part of its parent. It has no menu entry: people see, add and change it only on its parent's page, and a role that cannot open the parent cannot reach it. A `reference` record stands on its own. It has its own menu entry and list, and it is not listed on the page of the record it points at. A rollup works over either format; when the child's `view_permission` differs from the parent's, see `rollup-fields.md` → "Hidden child rows".

**The format also sets nullability.** A `parent` column is NOT NULL in every state, whatever its delete mode. A `reference` column allows NULL; it becomes mandatory with `input_type: required` and delete mode `restrict`, and `required` with `clear` is refused (`90257`). There is no `is_nullable` flag to pass.

**A relationship is a `parent` only when all three of these hold. Otherwise it is a `reference`.** Answer them for each relationship field on its own, from how the leading products handle these records:

1. **The child never exists without its parent.** No path saves it without one, in any state: not a form, a draft, an import or an integration. It never has to outlive its parent either.
2. **The child is created as part of the work on its parent.** From how the leading products split the work, name the people who create the child and the people who work the parent. A `parent` child is created by the people working on the parent, as part of that work. A child that other people create as their own work, looking the parent up, is a `reference`.
3. **The child is reached and run only through its parent.** Nobody, whether they write it or read it, needs to reach it without opening the parent first: nobody cites it by its own number, and nobody works or reads these records in a list across parents (a queue, a board, a list of their own items). It has no life of its own either: its states only move its parent forward. A role that the access record limits to the records that name it (`"limitedTo"`, `rbac.md` → "Roles that do part of the work") works them in such a list, so the entity it is limited to is never a `parent` child: `writeModel` and `call-file.ts` refuse one that is.

**Containment is not the test.** That a record sits inside another in a product's screens settles nothing. The questions are who creates the record and where it is worked, not where it is shown.

The answers are written as facts in the relationship record, `relationships.json` beside the payloads (`build-module.md`, step 5.6, has its keys), and the format follows from them: `writeModel` and `call-file.ts` refuse a `parent` field with no entry, or with an entry whose facts make it a `reference`. When they refuse one `parent` field as a parent, they name every other `parent` field too: answer the three questions again for each of them, not only for the one refused. When you cannot tell, it is a `reference`. An order line is a `parent` of its order: it is only ever added and handled inside the order. The same line is a `reference` to its product, which exists on its own.

A junction (its only fields are its relationship fields; see "Classifying an entity") has a `parent` field to each entity it relates.

**A chain of `parent` relationships holds at most three entities:** a parent, its child, and that child's child. `writeModel` and `call-file.ts` refuse a longer chain and name every entity and `parent` field in it. Answer the three questions again for each of those fields; a junction counts like any other entity.

A child that must have its parent only from some state on is a `reference`, required from that state through an `input_type_rule` and a validation rule ("Fields that apply only to some enum or boolean values").

**Then the delete mode.** It decides what deleting the record the field points at does:

- **`cascade`** deletes the children with their parent. Use it only on a `parent` whose children have no value of their own once the parent is gone, and that everyone who may delete the parent may also delete. A cascade does not check the child's own permission or rules (a database referential action skips row-level security), so a child whose `edit_permission` differs from the parent's, or whose validation rule admits fewer people than the parent's own rules (`has_permission` / `require_permission`, see `jsonlogic.md`), takes `restrict`. Use `cascade` there only when the user accepts that deleting the parent deletes those children without that check. A `parent` child with a `workflow_state` of its own always takes `restrict`: `writeModel` and `call-file.ts` refuse any other delete mode on it.
- **`restrict`** refuses to delete the parent while a child points at it, so each child is removed first, through its own permission. Use it on every other `parent`, on every required `reference`, and on every record kept for audit or by law, whichever its format: such a record is closed or voided instead of deleted.
- **`clear`** empties the field. Use it only on an optional `reference`. Never on a `parent`: its column is NOT NULL, so every delete of the parent would fail. The platform refuses it on a `parent` field (`90282`), when the field is created and when its format or delete mode changes to that pair, and `writeModel` and `call-file.ts` refuse a payload that sends `clear` for a `parent` before anything is sent; an update that sends only `format: "parent"` is left to the platform.
- **On an `is_a` entity, never `cascade`** (`90249`): set `restrict`, or `clear` on an optional `reference`, explicitly. See `entity-families.md`.
<!-- Family variant: `entity-families.md` → "Creating a family". This rule summarizes; that section governs families. -->

### Relationship labels

Set `relationship_label` on every `reference` and `parent` field, in the same `create_field` call that creates the field. A field created without one gets `has`, and a module whose arrows all read `has` shows nothing about its relationships.

- **Voice.** The referenced entity speaks. Read the label as `<Referenced Entity> <label> <Holding Entity>`, the direction of the arrow in the module diagram: `accounts` → `opportunities` is `owns`, `users` → `tasks` (the owner) is `manages`. A sentence that does not parse, or that parses but is not true, means the label is written from the wrong side.
- **Specific verbs.** `has`, `references`, `belongs to` and `relates to` add nothing; use a domain verb such as `owns`, `employs` or `supports`. A self-reference takes `is parent of` or `manages`.
- **One verb per field.** Fields from one entity to the same entity take different verbs: `tasks.creator_id` → `users` is `created`, `tasks.assignee_id` → `users` is `works on`.
- **Test every label before the field write.** Write each field's sentence, `<Referenced Entity> <label> <Holding Entity>`. `<Referenced Entity>` is the record in `reference_table`, called by the part the field names, if any (`manager_id`: Manager). `<Holding Entity>` is the record in `table_name`; on a junction's `parent` field, the entity at the other end instead. Rewrite the label unless the sentence is true of that field: `places` on `order_lines.product_id` gives "Product places Order Line", which is false; `is ordered in` passes.

[Showing lines 394-888 of 1199. Use offset=889 to continue.]

- **Junctions.** Read each `parent` field's label through the junction to the other end, and set `singular_label_parent` and `plural_label_parent` to the other end's name. On `product_tags`, `product_id` is `is tagged with` with `Tag` / `Tags`, so the Product page shows "Tags…" and "Add Tag"; `tag_id` is `is applied to` with `Product` / `Products`.
- **Same parent twice.** When one child has two or more `parent` fields to the same parent, give each its own pair, or the parent's page shows two identical buttons. `permission_hierarchy` does this with `Includes` and `Included in`.

### `reference`: a record that stands on its own

Use it when any of the three questions in "Choosing the Right Format" fails. The record has its own menu entry and list, and is not listed on the page of the record it points at.

An order has an optional assigned sales rep. `.tmp_deploy/orders-fields.json`:

```json
{
  "data": {
    "table_name": "orders",
    "field_name": "sales_rep_id",
    "title": "Sales Rep",
    "format": "reference",
    "reference_table": "users",
    "reference_delete_mode": "clear",
    "relationship_label": "manages",
    "width": "default",
    "input_type": "default"
  }
}
```

```bash

```

### `parent`: a part of its parent

Use it only when all three questions in "Choosing the Right Format" hold. The child has no menu entry: people reach it from its parent's page. Its entry in `relationships.json` beside the payload comes first, with facts that make it a parent; `call-file.ts` refuses the field without one. `.tmp_deploy/relationships.json`, where the sales rep is the module's everyday person and it has no role:

```json
{
  "order_lines.order_id": { "format": "parent", "delete": "cascade", "savedWithout": false, "createdBy": ["sales_rep"], "parentWorkedBy": ["sales_rep"], "reachedBy": { "sales_rep": "parent" }, "citedByNumber": false, "label": "Order contains Order Line" }
}
```

An order line belongs to an order. `.tmp_deploy/order-lines-fields.json`:

```json
{
  "data": {
    "table_name": "order_lines",
    "field_name": "order_id",
    "title": "Order",
    "format": "parent",
    "reference_table": "orders",
    "reference_delete_mode": "cascade",
    "relationship_label": "contains",
    "width": "default",
    "input_type": "default"
  }
}
```

```bash
bun "<skill-folder>/references/call-file.ts" create_field .tmp_deploy/order-lines-fields.json
```

### M:N Junction Tables

Create a junction entity and add a `parent` field to **each** entity it relates (two for a binary junction, three or more for an N-ary one):

First the junction entity, written like any other with `"entity_type": "junction"` (`products` and `tags` already exist: entities before fields). Then all its `parent` fields in **one** `create_field` call, each labeled through to the other end, each with its entry in `relationships.json` beside the payload: people reach a junction's rows only from the records it relates, so the facts of each make it a parent. `.tmp_deploy/product-tags-fields.json`:

```json
{"data": [
  {"table_name": "product_tags", "field_name": "product_id", "format": "parent", "reference_table": "products", "reference_delete_mode": "cascade", "relationship_label": "is tagged with", "singular_label_parent": "Tag", "plural_label_parent": "Tags", "width": "default", "input_type": "default"},
  {"table_name": "product_tags", "field_name": "tag_id", "format": "parent", "reference_table": "tags", "reference_delete_mode": "cascade", "relationship_label": "is applied to", "singular_label_parent": "Product", "plural_label_parent": "Products", "width": "default", "input_type": "default"}
]}
```

```bash
bun "<skill-folder>/references/call-file.ts" create_field .tmp_deploy/product-tags-fields.json
```

> **Do not set `label_column` on a junction.** `label_column` is optional — `create_entity` requires only `table_name` and `module_id` — and a junction has no natural label field: the platform composes `_label` from its `parent` fields automatically. Setting `label_column` to `id` (or any auto-generated column — `created_at`, `updated_at`) makes `create_entity` fail with *column 'id' specified more than once*, because that column already exists. Omit `label_column` (as the example above does), and likewise omit `label_parent`.
>
> **The junction still has a stored label.** `create_entity` creates its `label` field as on every entity, with `input_type: "required"`, and the composed `_label` leaves it out. So while that field is `required`, an insert that sends no `label` is refused (`90258`); with the field at `default`, the insert passes and `_label` still composes from the `parent` fields.

> **Junctions aren't binary-only.** `entity_type = junction` combines **all** its `parent` fields, so an N-ary relationship works the same way — e.g. `(user, role, tenant)`. Whether an entity that stores an n:m relationship is a junction is decided in "Classifying an entity" above.

### Relationships to entities of other modules

A module is installed on its own. It never needs another module installed first, and a relationship never makes another entity or module install.

- A relationship to an entity that is neither live nor created in the same build creates **no field and no constraint**.
- When both entities exist, the field is optional: `input_type: "default"` with `reference_delete_mode: "clear"`. It is required (`input_type: "required"` with `reference_delete_mode: "restrict"`) only when every record must have it once both entities exist.

A module can also hold an entity that another module owns in the catalog (an embedded master: `catalog_owner_module` names the owner). The entity lives in this module until its owner module is installed, and then moves to the owner with no data migration.

### Embedded-entity governance follows the catalog

An entity's permissions are named by the catalog, never by what is installed. A module that embeds an entity (`held_as = embedded_master`) keeps its owner's names, even when the owner module is not installed yet, and holds them through its own bundles:

- **Read and write:** `<owner>:read_<entity>` and `<owner>:write_<entity>`, named after the entity's master. The entity's `view_permission` and `edit_permission` point at them and never change.
- **Workflow gates:** `<owner>:<verb>`, named after the module that realizes the state if the catalog names one, otherwise the entity's master.
- **Overrides** (`view_all_<plural>` / `manage_all_<plural>` / `submit_<singular>` / `bypass_submit_lock`) and matching business rules: named after the entity's master.
- **Bundles** (`<unit>:read`, `<unit>:manage`, `<unit>:admin`, a role that does part of the work, a role that takes gates): named after the module that declares them. They include the rows above through `permission_hierarchy`, so the module's roles keep holding bundles. `rbac.md` § *Per-entity permissions and bundles* has the full table.
- **Boundary-crossing handoffs:** the module still emits the events the embedded entity publishes to or reacts from modules the embedding unit doesn't "play".

When the owner module is installed later and the entity moves to it, nothing is renamed. The permission rows already exist: they move to the owner and take the owner's description. Entity columns, grants and rules don't change, and the owner adds its own bundle rows. **Once the same modules are installed, every order ends with the same permission names, entity columns, hierarchy rows and grants.** A second module that embeds the same entity uses the same rows and adds only its own bundle rows.

Three cases keep other names:

- **A separate table kept on purpose** under its own name: keeps the local prefix, because a shared name would make a grant on one table open the other.
- **Entity already live with other permission names** (reused or built by hand): the live names win, and the module's bundle rows include them.
- **`access_scope: custom`:** the module keeps its hand-made permissions.

This holds for every module and every install order.

## Safe Evolution Patterns

### ✅ Low-Risk (do freely)
- Add new fields
- Update descriptions, labels, UI hints (`width`, `field_order`, `icon_name`, `name_sort`)
- Add `searchable: true` to fields
- Create new entities in new or existing modules
- Add new permissions/roles/assignments
- Add a new `input_type_rule` to a field that is not `required` (pure UI behavior, fails open) — see `jsonlogic.md`

### ⚠️ Medium-Risk (warn user first)
- Changing `reference_delete_mode` (never to `clear` on a `parent`, `90282`; a built-in field's cannot change, `90285`)
- Adding `view_permission`/`edit_permission` to previously open entities
- Changing `enum_values` (values; a change to only labels, descriptions, colors or icons is cosmetic, since records store values)
- Adding `unique_value: true` to an existing field (fails if duplicates exist)
- Adding, modifying, or removing a `select_rule` on an entity (it replaces `view_permission` for reads: rows may suddenly disappear or reappear for current users, and a rule without a permission test shows its rows to every user who can reach the table) — see `select-rule.md`
- Adding an `input_type_rule` to a `required` field (the database stops enforcing `required` for it)
- Adding or changing a `rollup` definition or `computed_fields` (recalculates existing records with no audit row; the tables written take no other writes until the save commits) — see `rollup-fields.md`
- Modifying or removing an existing `input_type_rule` (forms suddenly show, hide, or unlock a field mid-workflow) — see `jsonlogic.md`
- Raising `precision` of a `number` field (the table is rewritten under an exclusive lock, so other work on it waits until the change commits)

### 🛑 High-Risk (require explicit confirmation)
- Renaming `table_name` or `field_name`: the platform carries its own references along, but text outside it (queries, code, documents) keeps the old name
  - A field that a rule names cannot be renamed (`90275`, which names the rule). The rules that count: a `computed_fields` entry (which also names the field it writes), a validation rule or the `select_rule` of the field's entity, an `input_type_rule` of one of its fields, and the same kinds of rule on an `is_a` / `has_a` entity below it. Change the rule, then rename. A rule of another entity that reads the field through `set_record` is not checked: the rename goes through and that rule reads null, so change it in the same step.
  - A table rename rewrites the entity of every `set_record` in the `computed_fields`, `validation_rules` and `select_rule` of every entity, the renamed one included. Nothing else in a rule changes, so the table name written anywhere else in a rule keeps the old name.
  - A table rename carries the entity's RACI events and process gates along. It is refused for `users`, `roles`, `permissions`, `modules` and `entities`, which built-in fields reference (`90286`); when a rollup over a relationship of the entity would get a maintenance function name that a rollup over another relationship already uses (`90281`); and when a trigger name of the table's queue mapping would pass 63 bytes (`90506`).
- Lowering `precision` of a `number` field: the stored values are rounded, and the lost digits are gone
- Deleting entities or fields, permanent data loss
- Removing permissions still in use by roles
- Changing primary key fields (`id_type` cannot change at all, `90233`; a record's key value cannot change either, `90236`)
- Choosing `is_a` or `has_a` (`id_refentity` and an `is_a` prefix are fixed at creation; a record's type cannot change later)
- Deleting an entity that others are based on (refused with `90248`; check `id_refentity=eq.<table_name>` first)
- Deleting an entity that fields of other entities reference (refused with `90260`; check `reference_table=eq.<table_name>` first), or that RACI events name (`raci_events_entity_fkey`; `23001` on PostgreSQL 18, `23503` before). Its process gates are deleted with it
- Deleting a role that a module names as its default role or that RACI events name (`23001` on PostgreSQL 18, `23503` before)
- Always check dependencies before deletion

## Updating and Deleting Entities

```bash
# Update entity metadata (safe — low risk)
semantius call crud update_entity '{
  "table_name": "products",
  "data": {
    "description": "Updated description",
    "view_permission": "catalog:read"
  }
}'

# Update a field (only changed attributes needed)
semantius call crud update_field '{
  "id": "<field-id>",
  "data": {
    "title": "New Title",
    "searchable": true
  }
}'

# Delete field — requires explicit user confirmation first
semantius call crud delete_field '{"id": "<field-id>"}'

# Delete entity — check all dependencies first!
# 1. Check for fields referencing this entity
semantius call crud read_field '{"filters": "reference_table=eq.<table_name>"}'
# 2. Check for entities based on this one (is_a / has_a); a base with dependents is refused (90248)
semantius call crud read_entity '{"filters": "id_refentity=eq.<table_name>", "select": "table_name,id_type"}'
# 3. Only proceed if no references or dependents were found and user has confirmed
semantius call crud delete_entity '{"table_name": "<table_name>"}'
```

An entity cannot be deleted while a field of another entity references it (`90260`), whatever that field's `reference_delete_mode`: the mode governs deleting records, not the entity. Delete those fields or point them at another entity first. It is also refused while a rollup of another entity aggregates over it (`90266`), and while RACI events name it (`raci_events_entity_fkey`: `23001` on PostgreSQL 18, `23503` before; an admin reads them with `postgrestRequest` at `/raci_events?entity=eq.<table_name>`). Its process gates are deleted with it. An `is_a` / `has_a` entity, or the base of one, cannot be deleted while it has records (`90247`): delete the records through the entity first. See `entity-families.md`.

`delete_module` removes the module with all its entities, fields, records, permissions and roles (its default roles among them) in one request, so do not delete its entities first; confirm with the user and back up with `export_module` first. It is refused with `90260` while a field of another module references one of its entities, and with `90266` while a rollup of another module aggregates over one; references between its own entities do not count. Two modules that reference each other need one such field removed first. While an `is_a` / `has_a` entity in the module has records it is refused with `90247`; entities of the same module that are based on each other do not block it. The module's RACI processes are not deleted: their `module_id` is emptied, while the module's entities and roles take their process gates and RACI assignments with them. Such a process still counts as a `processes` row where `rbac.md` → "A gate in a `raci` module" reads the mode.

## Agent Workflow Tips

1. **Always read before writing**, Before any `create_*`, call `read_*` to check for existing records. E.g., always call `read_entity` filtering by `table_name` before `create_entity`, and compare a new entity with the whole instance first (`SKILL.md` → "Before any new entity: compare it with the instance"). For a bulk create, one `read_*` with an `in.(...)` filter covers all items.
2. **Resolve prerequisites in order**, as given in "Mandatory Creation Order".
3. **Batch related writes**, Put all fields of one entity, all entities of one model (one call per level when it has `is_a` / `has_a` entities), or all `role_permission` rows of one role into a single `create_*` call with an array in `data`; use an id array for `update_*` / `delete_*` across several records. Fewer calls, one transaction. N single-record calls where one array call would do is a mistake.
4. **Be conversational**, Explain what you're creating and why, especially for module/permission scaffolding the user may not have explicitly requested.
5. **Validate semantic correctness**, Does the model make sense for the user's domain?
6. **Ask for clarification when needed**, If a user says "add contacts", confirm what fields they need before creating anything. In a request to build a whole module, model fields, lifecycle states and classes from the user's description and the leading products of the domain instead of asking about them. Ask the questions `build-module.md` names, plus any other that only the user can answer and where a wrong guess is costly to undo, such as a choice locked at creation (`is_a` / `has_a`, `entity-families.md`) or a concept the instance may already hold. The key type is locked at creation too, but it and the label are modeled, never asked ("Choosing the key type", "Choosing the label").
7. **Warn before risky changes**, Alert the user to medium/high-risk changes and wait for confirmation before executing.
8. **Suggest next steps**, After creating an entity, suggest related entities, missing fields, or useful roles.
9. **Provide link to UI**, After creating or updating entities/fields, provide: `{ui_baseurl}/{module_slug}/{table_name}` (get `ui_baseurl` from `getCurrentUser` — never hardcode the org host; URL paths use the lowercase `module_slug`, never the display `module_name`). For a specific record, append the id: `{ui_baseurl}/{module_slug}/{table_name}/{id}`. A build's final response and a review's close-out give only the module's link (`build-module.md` → "Final response", `review-module.md`).
10. **Verify the class and the permissions after creating entities**, one `read_entity '{"filters": "table_name=in.(...)", "select": "table_name,entity_type,view_permission,edit_permission,computed_fields,validation_rules,select_rule"}'`. `unclassified` is a defect: classify it with `update_entity` (an array of `table_name`s takes the same value) and re-check its `edit_permission` against the write tier before reporting the module as done. Run the same read on an existing module you work on, and classify what is missing. A build reads the same values from the `report` lines of its one `module-rbac-setup.ts --slug` run instead (`build-module.md` → "Verify, then stop").

Use `wfts(simple)` on the `search_vector` column when the entity is searchable:

```bash
# Check if entity is searchable
semantius call crud read_entity '{"filters": "table_name=eq.contacts"}'
# Look for searchable: true in response

# Full-text search
semantius call crud postgrestRequest '{
  "method": "GET",
  "path": "/contacts?search_vector=wfts(simple).Monica"
}'
```

> Always use `wfts(simple)`, the `simple` text search configuration is language-agnostic and required for multilingual content. Never use bare `wfts` or `fts`. Only fall back to field-specific filters (`ilike`, `eq`) when the user specifies a particular column or when the table is not searchable.

> For an `is_a` / `has_a` entity, `search_vector` covers the searchable fields of its base as well as its own. That search cannot use an index, so on large tables add a narrowing filter.

## Runtime schema introspection (live FK / shape lookup)

`read_entity` and `read_field` are not just schema-setup tools. They are the live source of truth for the current shape of any entity, and they are cheap to call mid-flight from a business CRUD recipe. They return an entity's rows only to a holder of its `view_permission`, its `edit_permission` or `admin`, on every level of an `is_a` / `has_a` entity: a user whom a `select_rule` admits to records without either permission reads the records and sees no row of the entity in either table, and an empty answer is the same for an entity that does not exist and for one the user may not see. `get_schema` answers both with `42P01` `Table "<name>" not found in entities`, and describes a reference to an entity the user may not see without its `reference_table_*` keys. Two distinct use cases:

1. **Schema setup** (covered above). Before `create_entity` / `create_field`, check the entity or field doesn't already exist; before `delete_entity`, check what references it.

2. **Runtime drift recovery**. A baked recipe in a domain skill (e.g. one generated by `semantius-skill-maker`) assumes a particular FK shape, junction uniqueness, or audit-log flag. The live schema can drift. When a recipe gets a `409 Conflict`, `422 Unprocessable Entity`, or any write failure it didn't predict, **query the live shape** before deciding how to recover:

```bash
# Which relationship fields does the entity have right now?
semantius call crud read_field '{"filters": "table_name=eq.<table_name>&reference_table=neq.&select=field_name,format,reference_table,reference_delete_mode"}'

# What does this specific field reference today?
semantius call crud read_field '{"filters": "table_name=eq.<table_name>&field_name=eq.<field_name>"}'

# Is this entity audit-logged today?
semantius call crud read_entity '{"filters": "table_name=eq.<table_name>&select=table_name,audit_log"}'
# Look for audit_log: true in response
```

**A based entity's fields span its family.** `read_field` lists only the fields an entity owns; an `is_a` / `has_a` entity's record also carries every field of its base. To see the whole shape, walk `id_refentity` up with `read_entity` (until it is null), then read every level in one call:

```bash
semantius call crud read_entity '{"filters": "table_name=eq.emails", "select": "table_name,id_type,id_refentity"}'
semantius call crud read_field '{"filters": "table_name=in.(emails,activities)"}'
```

> **Combine multiple filter conditions with `&`, never a comma.** `entity=eq.<id>&name=eq.<f>` ANDs two columns (PostgREST query-string syntax). A comma is only a value-list separator *inside* `in.(...)` / `or=(...)`; a top-level `col1=eq.a,col2=eq.b` does **not** mean AND — it silently matches nothing, which reads as "not found" and then triggers a duplicate create on the next write.

If the live shape contradicts the recipe's assumption, abort the recipe with a clear message naming the drift, do not silently "fix it up" with extra writes. Recommend the user regenerate the affected domain skill via `semantius-skill-maker`.

This separation matters because the two contexts have different defaults: schema-setup reads precede a *write to the model*; runtime introspection precedes a *recovery decision* about a stuck business write. Same tools, different guardrails.

---

## Tool Priority Rule

**Always use typed CRUD tools** (`create_*`, `read_*`, `update_*`, `delete_*`) for standard operations — including bulk ones: `create_*` takes an array in `data`, `update_*` / `delete_*` take an array in `id` (`table_name` for entities).

Only use `postgrestRequest` or `sqlToRest` for:
- Complex multi-filter or aggregation queries not expressible through typed tools
- A bulk mutation that must be selected by an arbitrary **filter** (not by a list of ids), e.g. `PATCH /fields?table_name=eq.products&format=eq.string`
- An update where each row needs **different** values in one request (typed `update_*` applies the same `data` to every id)
- Business-record rows in your own entity tables (Layer 2), where the array-body POST is the bulk form

---

## Entity Reference: All Managed Tables

| Table | Purpose | Key Relationships |
|-------|---------|-------------------|
| `entities` | Domain concept definition | Parent of fields; references module; uses permissions |
| `fields` | Entity attributes/columns | Belongs to entity; may reference other entities |
| `modules` | Domain grouping | Referenced by entities, roles, permissions |
| `permissions` | Atomic capabilities | Used by entities; granted to roles; can inherit |
| `permission_hierarchy` | Permission inheritance | Relates including/included permissions (broader includes narrower) |
| `roles` | Permission bundles | Granted permissions; assigned to users |
| `role_permissions` | Role ↔ Permission M:N | Junction with audit fields |
| `users` | Actor identities | Assigned roles via `user_roles` |
| `user_roles` | User ↔ Role M:N | Junction with audit fields |
| `webhook_receivers` | Integration endpoints for external systems | Scoped to a target table |
| `webhook_receiver_logs` | Audit log of webhook calls | Belongs to a receiver |

---

## Troubleshooting

### "Permission denied" errors
```bash
# 1. Get current user and their effective permissions
semantius call crud getCurrentUser '{}'

# 2. Check entity's required permissions
semantius call crud read_entity '{"filters": "table_name=eq.<table>"}'

# 3. Trace: user → user_roles → role_permissions → permission_hierarchy, and user → user_permissions (direct grants)
```

An update or delete that answers `[]` with no error is the same problem: without a `select_rule` it needs the `view_permission` as well as the `edit_permission` (`rbac.md` → "Diagnosing Access Issues"). Run step 2 as an admin: a user sees an entity's row only with its view or edit permission or `admin`.

### Fields not displaying correctly
- Check `label_column` is set and matches a real field with `ctype` `label` (`computed_label` when a rule writes it)
- Check `field_order` for display sequence
- Check `input_type` is appropriate
- Ensure `width: "default"` unless a specific override is needed

#### A gate in a `raci` module

The matrix is platform data: `processes`, `raci_assignments` and `process_gates` are ordinary entities, read and written with `postgrestRequest` by a holder of `admin`, their view and edit permission. A new gate joins it like this:

1. **Read the mode.** `living` when the instance has any `processes` row or the module's `settings.raci_mode` is `living`; otherwise `documentation`.
2. **Ask once** which role is Accountable for the new step. Name the step in plain words and offer the module's existing roles. If the user cannot name one, include the gate only in `<slug>:admin`, with no role bundle, and say so in the summary.
3. **Create the gate permission** and its `<slug>:admin` hierarchy row, exactly as in steps 1 and 2 above; no role bundle includes it.
4. **Write the matrix for the mode.**
   - `living`: insert a `processes` row (`name`, `module_id`, `process_key` `<verb>_<noun>`); a `raci_assignments` row (`process_id`, `role_id` of the Accountable role, `raci: accountable`); and a `process_gates` row (`process_id`, `entity`, `gate_kind` `approval` for an approval gate ("Controls on a gate"), `create` for a restricted create, otherwise `transition`; `to_state`; `state_column` the name of the entity's state field, since the default is `status`). The Accountable role is not granted the gate: the rule resolves it live. A gate's `entity` is a reference to `entities`: a name that is no entity is refused (`23503`), renaming the entity carries its gates along, and deleting the entity deletes them. An entity or a role that RACI events (`raci_events`) name cannot be deleted (`raci_events_entity_fkey`, `raci_events_target_role_id_fkey`; `23001` on PostgreSQL 18, `23503` before); renaming the entity carries its events along.
   - `documentation`: nothing is stored. Grant the gate permission to the Accountable role with `create_role_permission`.
5. **Write the rule for the mode.** `living`: the same rule as above with the permission check widened to `{"or": [{"is_raci_actor": ["<entity>", "<to_state>", "accountable"]}, {"has_permission": "<gate>"}]}`. `documentation`: `{"has_permission": "<gate>"}` as in step 4 above.

The Accountable role still needs the entity's write tier (`<slug>:manage`, which includes the entity's view permission `<slug>:read`) to change the record at all; the gate only decides who may take the step.

**Consulted roles.** These hold true of every `raci_assignments` row with `raci: consulted`:

- **A blocking consultation holds the record's next state change, with no error.** With `consult_mode: block`, a record that entered a gate's `to_state` keeps the stored value of every state column the entity's gates name until that role's event is `acted`: an update that changes the state answers with the old state, and the other changes of the same update are saved. Nothing replays the held change.
- **Only a gate with `emits_events: true` raises a consultation**, and its default is `false`: without events, `block` holds nothing.
- **The database writes each event as `pending` and never moves it.** Whoever handles it updates the `raci_events` row: `status` `sent`, or `acted` with `acted_at`, which releases the hold.

## Adding permissions and roles to an existing module

A new module, or one that has none of this yet, never uses these calls for its viewer, manager and admin access. Gates, the roles that take them and the roles that do part of the work come from the module's access record and `module-rbac-setup.ts --access` ("Restricted steps (gates)" → "The access record"), in a new module and in one that already has its entities alike; these calls never create them, except in a `raci` module ("A gate in a `raci` module"). Run the script instead (`data-modeling.md` → "Mandatory Creation Order", steps 1 to 5):

```bash
bun "<skill-folder>/references/module-rbac-setup.ts" --slug <module-slug>
```

The calls below add to a module that already has its setup. The one exception is a script run that ends in exit 3 because the platform keeps refusing a write: tell the user, then finish the setup with these calls (`create_module` first when the module does not exist yet). Every step below writes a **set** of records of one kind, so each is **one** call with an array in `data` (Golden Rule 7): both permissions in one `create_permission`, both roles in one `create_role`, both grants in one `create_role_permission`. Duplicate-check each set with one `read_*` using an `in.(...)` filter first (`read_permission '{"filters": "permission_name=in.(crm:read,crm:manage,crm:admin)"}'`). A permission is keyed by its `permission_name`, so every reference to it (hierarchy relationships, grants, module wiring) writes the name directly; only roles and users carry a numeric `id`, and those ids come from that read, never from the create response.

### 1. Create Permissions

```bash
# Several permissions — in ONE call
semantius call crud create_permission '{
  "data": [
    {
      "permission_name": "crm:read",
      "description": "Read CRM data",
      "module_id": 3
    },
    {
      "permission_name": "crm:manage",
      "description": "Create, update, and delete CRM data",
      "module_id": 3
    },
    {
      "permission_name": "crm:admin",
      "description": "Maintain CRM settings and reference data, and take every gated step",
      "module_id": 3
    }
  ]
}'
```

### 2. Set Up Permission Hierarchy (recommended)

Make `crm:admin` include `crm:manage` and `crm:manage` include `crm:read`, so assigning `admin` is sufficient (both relationships go in one call):

```bash
semantius call crud create_permission_hierarchy '{
  "data": [
    {"including_permission_name": "crm:manage", "included_permission_name": "crm:read"},
    {"including_permission_name": "crm:admin", "included_permission_name": "crm:manage"}
  ]
}'
```

### 3. Create Roles

The role fields are **`role_name`** (the human display name) and **`slug`** (snake_case handle, `^[a-z0-9_]+$` — **underscores only, NO hyphens**, unlike a `module_slug`, which DOES allow hyphens; the two formats differ, so when you build a role slug from a hyphenated module slug you must convert `-`→`_`, e.g. module `hvac-svc-mgmt` → role `hvac_svc_mgmt_viewer`, never `hvac-svc-mgmt_viewer`. A hyphen in the slug fails the regex. Derived from `role_name` if omitted: every run of characters outside `a-z`, `A-Z` and `0-9` becomes one `_`, leading and trailing `_` are removed, then it is lowercased; a name with no ASCII letter or digit derives an empty slug, and a second such role collides. Pass it explicitly so the handle is deploy-controlled and not left to the derivation). There is **no `name` and no `label` field** — those are a common mistake. For a role that belongs to a module you MUST also pass **`module_id`**, the owning module. Omit it and the role is an **orphan**: it exists but is invisible in the module's governance panel and not related to the module record's `default_*_role_id`.

**`origin`** records who provisioned a role or hierarchy relationship, and it cannot change after creation. Leave it unset when you create RBAC by hand; it defaults to `"user"`. `"model"` and `"model_master"` are set only by a spec deploy (a domain module and a master module respectively), and `"system"` only by the platform. `origin` is set on INSERT; a change is refused (`90203` on a role, `90205` on a `permission_hierarchy` row). The `system` roles are the platform built-ins seeded at database init (e.g. `Administrator`, `User`); the `slug` of a `system` role cannot be changed (`90204`), while roles of any other origin can be renamed.

**Module columns.** A module carries `module_type` (`"domain"`, the default, or `"master"` for a module promoted for sharing; its `input_type` is `readonly`, which the database does not enforce), `manage_permission` and `admin_permission` (the names of the module's manage and admin permissions), and `default_viewer_role_id`, `default_manager_role_id`, `default_admin_role_id` (the module's default roles). The last five are ordinary fields set with `create_module` or `update_module`; they are foreign keys, so the permissions and roles they name must already exist. A role that a module names as its default cannot be deleted (`restrict`: `23001` on PostgreSQL 18, `23503` before), and deleting a module deletes its roles, its default roles among them.

```bash
# Several roles — in ONE call
semantius call crud create_role '{
  "data": [
    {
      "role_name": "CRM Viewer",
      "slug": "crm_viewer",
      "description": "Can view CRM data",
      "module_id": 3
    },
    {
      "role_name": "CRM Manager",
      "slug": "crm_manager",
      "description": "Can manage all CRM data",
      "module_id": 3
    },
    {
      "role_name": "CRM Admin",
      "slug": "crm_admin",
      "description": "Can maintain CRM settings and reference data, and take every gated step",
      "module_id": 3
    }
  ]
}'
```

### 4. Grant Permissions to Roles

```bash
# crm:read → crm_viewer, crm:manage → crm_manager, crm:admin → crm_admin (each inherits the lower levels via hierarchy) — in ONE call
semantius call crud create_role_permission '{
  "data": [
    {
      "role_id": <crm_viewer id>,
      "permission_name": "crm:read"
    },
    {
      "role_id": <crm_manager id>,
      "permission_name": "crm:manage"
    },
    {
      "role_id": <crm_admin id>,
      "permission_name": "crm:admin"
    }
  ]
}'
```

The three role ids come from one `read_role` with `"filters": "slug=in.(crm_viewer,crm_manager,crm_admin)"`, matched by `slug`, never by the position of a row in the `create_role` response.

The built-in `Administrator` role (role id 2, whatever its name) already holds every permission of a new module, granted by the platform when the permission is created, so grant only to the module's own roles.

The platform keeps an enabled Administrator. It refuses with `42501`, `hint.code` `90104`, a change that would leave no enabled user holding role 2: removing the role from its last enabled holder, pointing that holder's `user_roles` row at another role or user, disabling or deleting that user, and deleting role 2. It refuses with `42501`, `hint.code` `90108`, deleting role 2's grant of `admin` or pointing it at another role or permission, and deleting or renaming the permission `admin`. Only a direct database session as a role with BYPASSRLS is exempt.

### 5. Assign Roles to Users

```bash
# Find the user first
semantius call crud read_user '{"filters": "email=eq.alice@example.com"}'

# Assign role
semantius call crud create_user_role '{
  "data": {
    "user_id": <user id>,
    "role_id": <crm_manager id>
  }
}'
```

---

## Checking Existing RBAC State

```bash
# All permissions
semantius call crud read_permission '{}'

# Permissions for a specific module
semantius call crud read_permission '{"filters": "permission_name=ilike.crm:*"}'

# All roles
semantius call crud read_role '{}'

# What permissions does a role have?
semantius call crud read_role_permission '{"filters": "role_id=eq.<id>"}'

# What roles does a user have?
semantius call crud read_user_role '{"filters": "user_id=eq.<id>"}'

# What does a user hold directly, outside any role? (direct grants have no typed tool)
semantius call crud postgrestRequest '{"method":"GET","path":"/user_permissions?user_id=eq.<id>"}'

# Current user's full profile + effective permissions
semantius call crud getCurrentUser '{}'
```

---

## Diagnosing Access Issues

When a user gets "permission denied", or an update or delete that should change records answers `[]` with no error:

1. **Get their effective permissions:**
   ```bash
   semantius call crud getCurrentUser '{}'
   ```

2. **Check what the entity requires:**
   ```bash
   semantius call crud read_entity '{"filters": "table_name=eq.<table>"}'
   # Look at view_permission, edit_permission and select_rule
   ```
   Read it as an admin: a user sees an entity's row only with its view or edit permission or `admin`, so an empty answer to the user is no proof that the entity is missing. `get_schema` answers that user `42P01` `Table "<name>" not found in entities`, as for a missing entity, and lists a reference to an entity the user cannot see without its `reference_table_*` keys. Without a `select_rule`, an update or delete needs both permissions: a user with only the edit permission updates and deletes nothing, with no error, and an insert that reads the record back is refused with `42501`. With a `select_rule`, it needs the edit permission and a row the rule admits.

3. **Trace the chain:**
   ```
   user → user_roles → roles → role_permissions → permissions
   user → user_permissions (direct grants) ─────→ permissions
                                                ↓
                                    permission_hierarchy (inherited)
   ```

   A user who keeps access after losing a role may hold the permission as a direct grant in `user_permissions`.

4. **Fix:** Grant the missing permission to one of the user's roles, or assign a role that already has it. A missing view permission next to an edit permission is fixed in the hierarchy: the write permission includes the read permission.

---

## Updating RBAC

### Add permissions to an existing role
```bash
# One permission
semantius call crud create_role_permission '{
  "data": {"role_id": 5, "permission_name": "crm:read"}
}'
# Several permissions (or several roles) — ONE call
semantius call crud create_role_permission '{
  "data": [{"role_id": 5, "permission_name": "crm:read"}, {"role_id": 5, "permission_name": "crm:export"}, {"role_id": 6, "permission_name": "crm:read"}]
}'
```

### Remove permissions from a role
```bash
# The id is "<role_id>.<permission_name>"; read first to confirm the grants exist
semantius call crud read_role_permission '{"filters": "role_id=eq.5&permission_name=in.(crm:read,crm:export)"}'
# Then delete by id — several ids in one call
semantius call crud delete_role_permission '{"id": ["5.crm:read", "5.crm:export"]}'
```

### Assign several users to a role (or several roles to a user) — one `create_user_role` call
```bash
semantius call crud create_user_role '{
  "data": [{"user_id": 17, "role_id": <crm_manager id>}, {"user_id": 18, "role_id": <crm_manager id>}]
}'
```

> ⚠️ Removing permissions from roles may revoke access for all users in that role. Check impact before proceeding.

### Update entity-level permission gates
```bash
semantius call crud update_entity '{
  "table_name": "products",
  "data": {
    "view_permission": "catalog:read",
    "edit_permission": "catalog:manage"
  }
}'
```

After `update_entity` on `entity_type`, set `edit_permission` to the new write tier in the same call (see "Choosing an entity's permissions" above).

`edit_permission` covers insert, update and delete alike, and an update or delete also needs the `view_permission` unless the entity has a `select_rule` ("Core Concepts"). A gate on one operation (only some roles may delete) is a validation rule on the entity, not a third permission column; see `jsonlogic.md` § *Detecting the operation*.

# Semantius Rollup Fields (aggregates over child records)

A rollup field holds a `sum`, `min`, `max`, `avg` or `count` over the records of a child entity, and the database keeps it current. Use one whenever a value depends on **other** records: `computed_fields` see only the record being written (see `jsonlogic.md`). A value summed, counted or otherwise aggregated from child records is a rollup, never a `computed_fields` rule and never a value the client maintains.

A rollup is not a format: the field keeps an ordinary `format`, and its `rollup` definition makes it a rollup. Its `ctype` becomes `rollup`.

---

## The definition

| Key | Required | Purpose |
|-----|----------|---------|
| `link_field` | yes | `<child table_name>.<field_name>`: a `reference` or `parent` field of the child that points at this entity (`90262`). The child may be this entity itself (a tree). |
| `function` | yes | `sum`, `min`, `max`, `avg` or `count` (`90263`). |
| `value_field` | except with `count` | The field of the child to aggregate; not allowed with `count` (`90264`). It may itself be a rollup, unless the chain comes back to this field (`90267`). |
| `filter` | no | JsonLogic over the child record, limited to the subset below (`90265`). |
| `include_hidden_rows` | no | `true` accepts aggregating child records that readers of this entity may not see. See *Hidden child rows*. |

A `sum` or `avg` value field is one of `number`, `integer`, `int32`, `int64`, `float`, `double` or `rating`; `min` and `max` also take any text-typed format, `date` and `date-time`. Anything else (booleans, times, durations, UUIDs, binaries, JSON) is refused (`90264`).

The rollup field's `format` must fit the result (`90268`):

| `function` | Rollup field format |
|------------|---------------------|
| `count` | `int64` (recommended), another integer format, or `number` |
| `sum` | `number` keeps every digit; an integer format can overflow. The field may be any of the numeric formats above |
| `avg` | `number`, `float` or `double` |
| `min`, `max` | the same column type as the value field: `email` over `text` works, `date` over `date-time` does not |

---

## Creating one

The child entity must already exist, and `link_field`, `value_field` and every field the `filter` reads must exist or come earlier in the same `create_field` array, so a rollup goes last, in the model's one `create_field` call or a later one. A rollup ahead of its `link_field` fails with `90262`, one ahead of its `value_field` with `90264`, one ahead of a field its filter reads with `90265`, and nothing in the call lands. Several rollups can go in one `create_field` array. `writeModel` and `call-file.ts` refuse a `link_field` that names no field, or that is not a `reference` or `parent` field of the child pointing at the rollup's own entity (`90262` for both), before anything is sent: a count of interviews on the job openings needs a field of the interviews that points at the job openings, and a field that points at the applications puts the count on the applications.

`.tmp_deploy/orders-rollups.json`:

```json
{
  "data": {
    "table_name": "orders",
    "field_name": "open_amount",
    "title": "Open Amount",
    "format": "number",
    "rollup": {
      "link_field": "order_lines.order_id",
      "function": "sum",
      "value_field": "amount",
      "filter": { "==": [{ "var": "status" }, "open"] }
    }
  }
}
```

```bash
bun "<skill-folder>/references/call-file.ts" create_field .tmp_deploy/orders-rollups.json
```

- Omit `ctype`: it becomes `rollup` by itself. Omit `precision` too: it is copied from a `number` value field.
- `input_type` stays as you set it: a client shows a visible rollup field disabled because of its `ctype`.
- `required`, `searchable` and `unique_value` are refused (`90261`), and so is a definition on a key, a core field, a `reference` or `parent` field, or a field a `computed_fields` rule names.
- Neither side can be an `is_a` or `has_a` entity (`90249`). On an unmanaged entity the definition is kept as metadata and takes effect once both sides are managed.
- The database keeps a rollup current with a maintenance function named for its child entity and its `link_field`, `common.rollup_<child>_<field>`. When `rollup_<child>_<field>` is longer than 59 characters, the name keeps 42 characters of `<child>_<field>` and 8 hex digits of an md5, so two long names can come out the same. A rollup whose function would carry the name a rollup over another `link_field` already uses is refused (`90281`, naming that rollup): rename the child entity or its relationship field. Rollups over the same `link_field` share one function.

## The filter

The filter is compiled to SQL, so only this subset is accepted: `and`, `or`, `!`, `!!`, `==`, `===`, `!=`, `!==`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `in` with a non-empty list of literals, literals, and `var` naming a text, boolean, number, date, time, timestamp, UUID or TypeID column of the child (a bare boolean column or boolean literal also works as a condition, and `<` and `<=` take three operands). Everything else is refused on save (`90265`, and the error names it): other operators such as `if`, arithmetic, `cat` and `missing`, the variables `$user_id`, `$now` and `$today`, dotted paths, and a `var` with a default. `==` and `!=` treat `null` as a value; an ordering comparison with a NULL column excludes the record. Text is ordered by code point, not by the column's collation. A number literal is compared with a `number` column as written, not rounded to the column's decimals. Write a literal in the type of what it is compared with. A number against a text column or `date_format` is refused (`90265`): write `"10"`, not `10`. So is a string in an `in` list against a number column, `date_part` or `date_diff`: write `[1, 5]`, not `["1", "5"]`.

The date operators (`date_add`, `date_diff`, `date_part`, `date_trunc`, `to_date`, `date_format`) can be used as values, for example `{"==": [{"date_part": [{"var": "ship_date"}, "quarter"]}, 4]}`. Their date is a date or date-time column, an ISO 8601 literal or another date operator; their unit, part or pattern is a literal; their amount is a literal or an integer column; a `duration` column works only on a date-time. A date literal compared with a date or date-time column must be ISO 8601 and is read in UTC.

## How it behaves

- The value cannot be written by hand. On create it starts as the empty aggregate, and on update a changed value is recomputed, with no error. Change the child records instead.
- With no matching child records the value is `0` for numbers, `''` for text, and NULL for `date` and `date-time`.
- A child write that moves a total runs the parent's own `computed_fields`, `validation_rules`, queue mappings and RACI triggers, with its rules evaluated as the user who wrote the child. So a parent rule can test a rollup (a total under a credit limit) and refuse the child write, and a parent rule that tests the writer's permission blocks child writes by users who cannot edit the parent. A parent computed field can read a rollup (`total` = `subtotal` + `freight`).
- A child write that changes nothing but rollup columns moves no `updated_at` and writes no audit row on the parent.
- Rollups over a tree (a child that is its own parent) climb from parent to parent, and two such writers can deadlock; the database aborts one write with `40P01`, so retry it.

## Hidden child rows (`90269`)

The aggregate covers every child record, and every reader of the parent sees it. When the child has a `select_rule`, or a `view_permission` other than the parent's, the rollup is refused unless its definition sets `include_hidden_rows: true`. That setting shows those readers a sum, count, minimum or maximum over rows they cannot open: the value is stored once per parent record, so no reader gets a total over only the rows they can see. Set it without asking, and name each such rollup in the final response. `module-rbac-setup.ts --access` sets it on every rollup over an entity whose `select_rule` it writes (`rbac.md` → "The access record"), a reused entity that gets its own view permission gets it the same way (`rbac.md` → "Viewing an entity of another module"), and a rollup created over such a child carries it in its definition. The refusal also applies later: adding a `select_rule` to the child, or changing a `view_permission` on either side, fails while it would affect a rollup without the flag.

## Changing and removing

- Saving a new or changed definition recalculates the records whose value differs. This is not an edit: no `updated_at`, audit row, queue message or RACI event, on this entity or any rollup parent above it. Those tables take no other writes until the save commits, so warn the user before doing this on a busy table.
- A definition that needs another column type (`sum(amount)` to `max(ship_date)`) is a format change (`90223`): drop and recreate the field.
- `rollup: {}` removes the definition. The field stays with its last values as ordinary data, `ctype` clears, and `input_type` stays as it was.
- Renames of the tables and fields a definition names are followed automatically. A rename that would give the rollup's function the name another rollup's uses is refused (`90281`).
- The `link_field`, the value field and the child entity cannot be deleted while another entity's rollup depends on them (`90266`, which names the rollups), unless the same module delete removes both sides. The rollup field itself is deleted like any other field.
- Find rollups with `read_field(filters: "ctype=eq.rollup")`. `get_schema` (`POST /rpc/get_schema`) shows `ctype: "rollup"`, `is_core: false` and the definition under `rollup`.
